review_notes: I read the whole file. I checked the many @[simp] dist/nndist lemmas for lineMap, homothety, midpoint and pointReflection for overlapping left-hand sides. I also checked them against the core simp lemmas lineMap_apply_zero, lineMap_apply_one, lineMap_apply_one_sub and homothety_apply_same, and against the AffineIsometryEquiv pointReflection lemmas in Isometry.lean. I found no loops or competing rules. homothety_eq_lineMap is not simp, so the homothety and lineMap families stay separate. dist_pointReflection_right and smulTorsor_ratio are correctly not simp, because 𝕜 and x, y cannot be inferred from their left-hand sides. The one finding is about the @[simps] interface of DilationEquiv.smulTorsor. I could not run Lean, so I did not observe the generated simp lemma. My claim about its shape rests on how simps handles non-lambda right-hand sides, and I am only moderately sure of it.

findings.problem: The def uses @[simps], but `invFun` is not written as a lambda. It is `k⁻¹ • (fun x => x -ᵥ c)`, a pointwise scalar action on a function. Unlike `toFun := (k • · +ᵥ c)`, the generated `smulTorsor_symm_apply` will therefore most likely be stated on the unapplied coercion, `⇑(smulTorsor c hk).symm = k⁻¹ • fun x => x -ᵥ c`. I have not run Lean to confirm this. If so, the simp normal form of `(smulTorsor c hk).symm p` goes through `Pi.smul_apply` and beta reduction instead of rewriting directly to `k⁻¹ • (p -ᵥ c)`. The simp interface for the inverse is then inconsistent with the forward direction.
findings.proposed_change: Write the inverse as an explicit lambda: `invFun := fun p => k⁻¹ • (p -ᵥ c)`. @[simps] should then produce an applied lemma `(smulTorsor c hk).symm p = k⁻¹ • (p -ᵥ c)`. The proofs `left_inv` and `right_inv` use `simp [...]` and should still go through. They may need a small adjustment, which I have not tested.
findings.benefit: Users of `DilationEquiv.smulTorsor` get a direct, applied simp lemma for the inverse that mirrors `smulTorsor_apply`. Their simp calls would not depend on `Pi.smul_apply` to unfold a function-level smul. The only downstream use I found is Tietze.lean, which uses the forward lemma `smulTorsor_apply`.
